title: Tile Shuffle
statement: A sliding puzzle has a 2 × 3 frame holding tiles 1 to 5 and one empty space shown as 0. A move slides a tile that is edge-adjacent to the empty space into it. Given the current board, return the fewest moves needed to reach [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 0]], or -1 if that arrangement cannot be reached.
constraints: board is 2 × 3 and contains each of 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 exactly once

examples.explanation: Slide 5 left into the space: one move.
Swapping two tiles is impossible with slides, so the answer is -1.

hints.content: Each arrangement of the board is a state; each slide is an edge between states.
There are only 6! = 720 arrangements, so you can afford to explore them all.
Breadth-first search from the starting arrangement finds the fewest moves.
Encode a board as a six-character string so it can go in a visited set; precompute which positions are adjacent to each position of the space.
If BFS finishes without reaching the target, return -1. (Exactly half of the arrangements are reachable, a parity argument.)

testCases.explanation: Slide 5 left into the space: one move.
Swapping two tiles is impossible with slides, so the answer is -1.
The space starts in the opposite corner.

solutions.title: Iterative deepening search
solutions.intuition: Try every move sequence of length 0, 1, 2, ... until one solves the board.
solutions.approach: Depth-limited DFS that avoids immediately undoing the previous move, increasing the limit until the target appears, up to the maximum possible distance.
solutions.pseudocode:
for limit in 0..31: if dfs(state, limit, none): return limit
return -1
commonMistakes: Running unbounded DFS, which wanders forever.
Not knowing the maximum distance (21 moves for this puzzle), so the unsolvable case never terminates.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Iterative deepening finds the shortest solution with tiny memory, but it re-explores shallow levels repeatedly and the branching blows up near the maximum depth.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.content: Limit 0: the start is not the goal.

solutions.title: Breadth-first search over board states
solutions.intuition: With only 720 states, BFS over all of them finds the minimum moves directly.
solutions.approach: Encode the board as a string. BFS from it: for each state, swap the space with each adjacent position (from a precomputed table), skip visited states, and return the layer number when the target appears.
commonMistakes: Encoding the board in a way that does not distinguish states (for example summing tiles).
Marking states visited when dequeued instead of enqueued, which duplicates work.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Treating each arrangement as a node turns the puzzle into a shortest path in an unweighted graph, so BFS gives the minimum. The state space is 720, so this is effectively constant time. For larger puzzles like the 15-puzzle I'd use A* with a Manhattan-distance heuristic, and check solvability up front with the permutation parity.
